prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that the improper joinder doctrine requires the removing party to show there is no reasonable basis to predict recovery against the in-state defendant.

Cite at least six decisions of the Fifth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

### I. Improper joinder requires the removing defendant to show that there is no reasonable basis to predict recovery against the in-state defendant.

Removal jurisdiction is strictly construed, and the removing party bears the burden of establishing it. The improper joinder doctrine is a narrow exception to the rule that complete diversity is required. *Smallwood v. Ill. Cent. R.R. Co.*, 385 F.3d 568, 572-73 (5th Cir. 2004) (en banc); *Flagg v. Stryker Corp.*, 819 F.3d 132, 136 (5th Cir. 2016) (en banc). A defendant may invoke that exception only by showing "actual fraud in the pleading of jurisdictional facts" or an "inability of the plaintiff to establish a cause of action against the non-diverse party in state court." *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 573. Only the second route is at issue here. This Court's en banc test for that route is exacting: the defendant must demonstrate "that there is no possibility of recovery by the plaintiff against an in-state defendant, which stated differently means that there is no reasonable basis for the district court to predict that the plaintiff might be able to recover against an in-state defendant." *Id.*; accord *Flagg*, 819 F.3d at 136; *Cuevas v. BAC Home Loans Servicing, LP*, 648 F.3d 242, 249 (5th Cir. 2011).

The burden is the removing party's, and it is a heavy one. *Travis v. Irby*, 326 F.3d 644, 649 (5th Cir. 2003) ("[T]he burden of persuasion on those who claim fraudulent joinder is a heavy one."); *Campbell v. Stone Ins., Inc.*, 509 F.3d 665, 669 (5th Cir. 2007); *Gasch v. Hartford Accident & Indem. Co.*, 491 F.3d 278, 281-82 (5th Cir. 2007). The defendant cannot meet it by showing that the plaintiff's claim is weak, that it may ultimately fail, or that the defendant disputes the facts. The question is whether the plaintiff has any reasonable prospect of success in state court. A "mere theoretical possibility of recovery" is not enough to defeat removal, *Great Plains Tr. Co. v. Morgan Stanley Dean Witter & Co.*, 313 F.3d 305, 312 (5th Cir. 2002), but the possibility Plaintiff must show is a reasonable one, and Plaintiff has shown it here.

The same standard governs how the Court evaluates the record. In deciding whether a reasonable basis exists, the Court must "evaluate all of the factual allegations in the light most favorable to the plaintiff, resolving all contested issues of substantive fact in favor of the plaintiff," and must resolve all ambiguities in controlling state law in the plaintiff's favor. *Travis*, 326 F.3d at 649 (citing *Burden v. Gen. Dynamics Corp.*, 60 F.3d 213, 216 (5th Cir. 1995)). The Court does not weigh evidence or decide the merits. *See McDonal v. Abbott Labs.*, 408 F.3d 177, 183 (5th Cir. 2005).

The ordinary method of testing the reasonable-basis question is a Rule 12(b)(6)-type analysis of the complaint. *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 573. "[I]f a plaintiff can survive a Rule 12(b)(6) challenge, there is no improper joinder." *Id.* In applying that analysis, the Court uses the federal pleading standard, asking whether the complaint states a plausible claim against the in-state defendant. *Int'l Energy Ventures Mgmt., L.L.C. v. United Energy Grp., Ltd.*, 818 F.3d 193, 200-02 (5th Cir. 2016). Summary-judgment-type evidence is appropriate only in the rare case in which a plaintiff has stated a claim but has misstated or omitted discrete facts that would determine the propriety of joinder. *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 573-74. Even then, the inquiry must not become a pretrial of the merits. *Id.* at 574.

Applying these principles, Defendants have not carried their burden. Plaintiff's complaint alleges [summarize the elements and facts pleaded against the in-state defendant, with citations to the record], and those allegations state a plausible claim under [state] law. Defendants do not contend that the complaint fails to plead the elements of that claim. Instead, they rely on [describe Defendants' evidence or arguments], which at most raises a factual dispute or a merits defense. Under *Travis*, such disputes must be resolved in Plaintiff's favor, and under *Smallwood*, they cannot support a finding of improper joinder. A defense that the in-state defendant may ultimately prevail does not establish that Plaintiff has no reasonable basis for recovery.

Because Defendants have not shown that there is no reasonable basis to predict that Plaintiff might recover against the in-state defendant, that defendant was properly joined. Complete diversity is therefore lacking, and the district court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction. The judgment should be vacated and the case remanded to state court.
